claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid solutions.
The initial nanoparticles have an FCC crystal structure.
High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by optimization of composition and atomic arrangement.
Combining experimental synthesis with DFT modeling can optimize nanoparticle composition and atomic arrangement.
The proposed synthesis intervention includes annealing at 1073 K for 2 hours.
The proposed annealing is conducted in an inert atmosphere with heating and cooling rates of 10 K/min and 5 K/min, respectively.
Optimized composition and atomic arrangement reduce lattice strain.
Optimized composition and atomic arrangement increase cohesive energy.
Reduced lattice strain and increased cohesive energy improve structural stability at high temperature.
Reduced lattice strain and increased cohesive energy improve chemical stability at high temperature.
The optimized nanoparticles will exhibit a 20% increase in structural stability relative to the conventional baseline.
The optimized nanoparticles will exhibit a 30% increase in chemical stability relative to the conventional baseline.
XRD can be used to quantify the claimed structural-stability increase.
EDS can be used to quantify the claimed chemical-stability increase.
The comparison baseline consists of conventionally synthesized nanoparticles without composition or atomic-arrangement optimization.
The nanoparticles remain stable from 773 to 1923 K for 100 hours.
The theoretical model may not fully capture nanoparticle behavior under the stated high-temperature service regimes.
An improvement of less than 10% relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
